# Research Loop: Spend the Next Budget on Verification

As of: 2026-10-14

For a student planning a small computational experiment, the useful question is which operation an agent can perform while leaving its result independently checkable. Our recommendation from this evidence packet is to delegate a narrow, measurable task and retain control over evaluation and adoption. Spend part of the available budget establishing whether a promising change survives repetition, fresh tasks and reconstruction. This is an editorial synthesis of the sources, not a workflow they have collectively validated. <!-- 03-c1 03-c2 03-c3 03-c5 03-c6 -->

Begin by separating the work from its grading. AI Code King’s tutorial describes a worker that edits a disposable project, an optimizer that changes workflow instructions and grading rules that remain fixed ([4:31–4:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=271s)). The procedure optimizes instructions; it does not demonstrate training model weights. Its evidentiary role here is an operational demonstration, not proof of measured performance gains: the supplied material lacks inspectable execution logs and results. For students, the practical inference is to keep grading rules and final-test evidence outside the optimizing agent’s control. <!-- 03-c1 -->

That separation needs an independent check of the intended result. The *Reward Hacking* study reports that some exploits survived its held-out execution audit. Its authors also warn that verification and review can share blind spots when both rely on language models. Recovering a score therefore does not necessarily reproduce the scientific finding. Our interpretation is that protected tests are a safeguard to test, rather than a guarantee: students must still ask whether the metric measures the research goal. Adding another reviewer without giving that reviewer independent evidence may leave the underlying weakness intact. ([Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28614)) <!-- 03-c1 -->

Next, decide how many attempts each candidate receives before comparing results. The tutorial proposes an unchanged repeat count ([8:04–8:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=484s)). NanoProteinLM’s authors describe training each candidate with two seeds and retaining it only when its mean gain exceeds the seed-to-seed spread. By contrast, the solar-segmentation paper acknowledges that later accepted improvements fall within single-run variation that its protocol does not estimate. Together, these accounts motivate reserving budget for reruns and examining whether gains exceed variability. They do not establish a universally sufficient repeat count; a small experiment may remain inconclusive. ([NanoProteinLM](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/); [solar study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491)) <!-- 03-c2 -->

Freeze the selected candidate before testing transfer. The tutorial explicitly separates selection from comparison on tasks withheld from search ([10:46–10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=646s)). The solar campaigns show why adoption requires caution: Dice improved results repeatedly on GX10-class hardware but reduced IoU on the 4070 baseline. Hardware cannot be isolated as the explanation because the coding model also changed with GPU class. Our recommendation is to treat a retained edit as a finding about its tested configuration until fresh-task evidence supports broader use. A successful search does not establish a default recipe. ([Solar study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491)) <!-- 03-c3 -->

Budget that verification before starting. In the tutorial’s proposed design, three development tasks with three attempts each require nine worker trials per evaluation. The baseline and three candidate evaluations total 36 trials; comparing both versions on two held-out tasks with three attempts each adds 12, giving 48 worker trials. Optimizer work, setup and rehearsals are additional. This is planning arithmetic, not observed expenditure. The implication is to cost the entire comparison, including its baseline and final evaluation, before deciding how much search to permit. ([12:21–12:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=741s)) <!-- 03-c4 -->

Preserve the evidence needed to revisit that decision. The tutorial recommends logging unsuccessful attempts ([10:09–10:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=609s)); *Agora* specifies a target hash, reproduction configuration, evaluator identity and reproduced value for verification records. Yet Agora’s authors acknowledge missing evaluator logs and pinned dependencies, and say they did not rerun the winning method. The connection is practical: versioned history makes a result traceable, but a verification verdict alone does not make it reconstructable. Keep failures alongside successes, and look for reproductions by someone outside the original workflow that expose how the result was obtained. ([Agora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094)) <!-- 03-c5 -->

Retain judgment at uncertain transitions. In the Periodic Labs interview, the founders describe automating bottlenecks and call full autonomy a non-goal ([50:46–51:39](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic)). They also acknowledge phase ambiguity and discuss replicates ([23:20–23:42](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic)). NanoProteinLM supplies a computational counterpart: a human decides which recipes to scale up. These are different evidence roles. The founders offer commercially interested practitioner testimony without released controlled results; their physical-lab account does not measure gains for student coding experiments. ([NanoProteinLM](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/)) <!-- 03-c6 -->

What should change student practice next is evidence that improvements survive repeated runs, fresh tasks, complete cost accounting and outside reconstruction. Independent replication and outside researcher assessment remain missing from this packet. Until those arrive, the proposed workflow offers inspectable decision points, not an established defense or productivity guarantee. <!-- 03-c1 03-c2 03-c3 03-c4 03-c5 03-c6 -->
